title: Sheets and Full-Screen Presentations
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of sheets and full-screen presentations in a Swift program or workflow.
Apply sheet presentation in a small, inspectable example.
Check the expected result and identify one boundary case or platform constraint.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on sheets and full-screen presentations and the practical choices around it. Start with the smallest example, connect it to “Sheet presentation”, and verify the result before adding complexity.
content.why_it_matters: Application code connects state, UI, APIs, data storage and platform capabilities. Clear ownership and explicit failure states make the experience more reliable and accessible.

content_blocks.title: Module 17: SwiftUI State, Architecture, and Application Flow
content_blocks.alt_text: Module 17: SwiftUI State, Architecture, and Application Flow. Lessons in order: State Management Fundamentals; The @State Property Wrapper; Bindings with @Binding; Observable Application Models; Observation and View Updates; Environment and Shared Dependencies; Reusable SwiftUI Components; Conditional Views and View Composition; Navigation State and Deep Linking; Sheets and Full-Screen Presentations; Lists with Editable Data; MVVM and Other App Architecture Patterns; Managing Complex App State.
content_blocks.caption: Numbered overview of the SwiftUI State, Architecture, and Application Flow learning sequence.

content_blocks.text: **Start with the rule.** For sheet presentation, separate app behavior from presentation and platform services. Define ownership and error states, test the behavior independently where possible, and verify Apple-platform requirements on a supported target.

**Work through the lesson.** Keep SwiftUI state ownership and data flow predictable while composing reusable screens and architecture. The detailed subtopic list in this lesson preserves the curriculum coverage; treat each item as a cue for a small example or a focused question rather than trying to memorize syntax.

content_blocks.text: Use the compiler and versioned documentation as evidence. Do not treat a source-string check or an illustrative output as proof that a complete Swift program compiles on every platform.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every Swift snippet can run in a browser or on every operating system.
common_mistakes.why: CodeLeaf’s current preview is not a Swift compiler, and Apple frameworks require appropriate target support.
common_mistakes.fix: Run command-line examples locally; use Xcode or a compatible package/target for framework-specific material.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating an illustrative output as compiler verification.
common_mistakes.why: A reference result helps reason about behavior but cannot replace compiling and testing the exact code.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example with the stated toolchain and test one realistic edge case.

common_mistakes.why: Swift concurrency checks and newer APIs can vary by language mode and toolchain.
common_mistakes.fix: Read the exact diagnostic and confirm the supported version before changing safety checks.
